opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So in late 2023 I was at Open Philanthropy, and we put out a request for proposals for benchmarks that measure how well LLM-based agents do on difficult, realistic tasks. The motivation came from a frustration I'd had for a while.

The benchmarks people were paying attention to were mostly multiple-choice or short-answer: MMLU, various reasoning and coding puzzles. They were getting saturated quickly, and even when a model hit 90% on one, it was hard to know what that meant for the real world. Does it mean the model can do a junior software engineer's job? Run a research project? Nobody could say, so you'd get people looking at the same numbers and drawing wildly different conclusions about how close we were to transformative AI.

What I cared about, from a forecasting and safety perspective, was whether these systems can autonomously carry out long, messy, multi-step work, the kind of thing that would let AI substantially automate AI research or economically important labor. That's the capability that matters for whether things go fast and whether we're prepared. And it's exactly what static Q&A benchmarks don't capture.

So the hope was to build evaluations where an agent has to complete tasks that take a skilled human hours or days, in realistic environments, with tools, where you can tell whether it actually succeeded. If you have those, a few good things follow.

First, you get a much more meaningful signal. Something like "this agent can complete 40% of tasks that take a professional engineer a full day" is something a policymaker or lab leader can reason about.

Second, you can track trends and extrapolate. If the length or difficulty of tasks agents can handle is growing at some steady rate, that's a far better basis for forecasting than vibes.

Third, it helps with the "if-then" style of governance people were starting to discuss: if a model crosses a certain capability threshold, then certain safeguards kick in. That only works if you can measure the threshold credibly before you cross it, not after.

And honestly, part of it was that I thought the field was going to be surprised. I suspected agent capabilities would improve faster than a lot of people expected once scaffolding and post-training caught up, and I wanted us to have good measuring sticks in place early, rather than scrambling to build them once the capabilities were already here.

r001.rationale: The response says existing evaluations were mostly multiple-choice or short-answer tests and describes the goal of building benchmarks where agents complete realistic, multi-step tasks, explicitly presenting this shift as the motivation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the short version is that in late 2023 I felt like the conversation about AI capabilities had gotten really untethered from anything you could actually measure. On one side you had people saying these systems were basically on the cusp of automating large chunks of knowledge work, and on the other side you had people pointing to the fact that if you actually tried to get GPT-4 to do a multi-step task on its own, it would wander off, forget what it was doing, make up a file that didn't exist. And both of those framings had something to them, but there was no shared yardstick. The existing benchmarks were almost all of the form "here's a question, give me an answer," and that just wasn't the thing I cared about. I cared about: can this system take a vague goal, operate over hours or days, use tools, recover from its own mistakes, and produce something a human would actually accept as finished work?

And the reason that mattered to me specifically is that so much of my thinking about timelines and about risk routes through the question of when AI starts meaningfully accelerating AI research itself. That's a very agentic activity. It's not answering trivia, it's running experiments, debugging, iterating, noticing when an approach is failing. So if I wanted to know how far we were from that, I needed evaluations that looked like that. Tasks that take a competent engineer or researcher a few hours to a few days, that have a real ground truth you can check against, and that aren't trivially memorizable from training data.

The other thing I was excited about was that realistic benchmarks give you traction on the disagreement itself. If I say "I think we're three years out" and someone else says "I think we're fifteen years out," we can argue forever. But if we both commit to a set of tasks and say "here's roughly what percentage success I'd expect by this date," then the world gets to adjudicate. And honestly I found I learned a lot just from the process of trying to write those tasks. You discover how much of your intuition about difficulty is wrong, how many tasks that feel hard are actually a lookup problem, and how many tasks that feel easy fall apart because they require sustained judgment. That was humbling in a useful way, and it's a big part of why I thought this was one of the highest-value things people could be working on at the time.

r001.rationale: Cotra contrasts question-and-answer benchmarks with realistic tasks requiring sustained tool use, error recovery, and finished work, identifying that shift as a reason for her enthusiasm.

astra-6.text:
What excited me was the possibility of measuring the gap between an AI that can give an impressive answer and an AI that can actually do a useful piece of work. Those are quite different things. A realistic task might require figuring out what to do, using tools, noticing that something has gone wrong, and recovering—all over a much longer stretch than answering a single question.

Difficult benchmarks seemed like a way to make that gap concrete. If an agent fails, is it missing some underlying capability, or does it need better tools or a better setup? And as systems improve, are they becoming more reliable at completing tasks that matter? I wanted measurements that would help us understand those changes, rather than just watching scores go up on tests that were already getting too easy.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts answering a single question with completing realistic work, but it does not identify multiple-choice tests as the evaluation method being replaced.

sol-6.1.text:
At the time, I felt like there was a pretty big gap between what models could do on existing benchmarks and what we actually wanted to understand about them. A model might do really well on a set of short questions, but that didn’t tell you whether it could carry out a complicated project over hours or days, deal with setbacks, and actually get something useful done.

I was excited about benchmarks that would put models in something closer to that situation: give them a realistic task, access to tools, and enough room to try things, and then see whether they succeeded. Where did they get stuck? Could they recognize a mistake and recover? Did they need a human to keep putting them back on track?

That seemed useful both for understanding the economic implications and for understanding risk. If we’re trying to anticipate when AI systems could automate substantial parts of research or other consequential work, we need measurements that connect to that work. And difficult benchmarks give you room to track progress before systems are already capable of doing everything you’re testing.

r001.rationale: The response explains enthusiasm for evaluating realistic, extended tasks rather than short questions, but it does not identify multiple-choice tests as the evaluation being shifted away from.
